title: 11  Transforming Your Data
section: 11.4 Example 3: Combine Select-All Boxes into One Variable (RACIALIZED)
text:
11.4 Example 3: Combine Select-All Boxes into One Variable (RACIALIZED)
The race/ethnicity question let people check more than one box, and Qualtrics exported one column per box: RACIALIZED_1 (American Indian or Alaska Native), RACIALIZED_2 (Asian), RACIALIZED_3 (Black or African American), RACIALIZED_4 (Hispanic or Latino), RACIALIZED_5 (Middle Eastern or North African), RACIALIZED_6 (Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander), RACIALIZED_7 (White), RACIALIZED_8 (Other, with the write-in in RACIALIZED_8_TEXT), and RACIALIZED_99 (Prefer not to say). A cell holds the option’s code when the box was checked and is blank (NA) otherwise. Look at a few rows first:

mh_clean |>
  select(RACIALIZED_1:RACIALIZED_99) |>
  head(8)

# A tibble: 8 × 9
  RACIALIZED_1 RACIALIZED_2 RACIALIZED_3 RACIALIZED_4 RACIALIZED_5 RACIALIZED_6
         <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>
1           NA            2           NA           NA           NA           NA
2           NA           NA           NA           NA            5           NA
3           NA           NA           NA            4           NA           NA
4           NA           NA           NA            4           NA           NA
5           NA           NA           NA           NA           NA           NA
6           NA            2           NA           NA           NA           NA
7           NA           NA           NA           NA           NA           NA
8           NA           NA           NA            4           NA           NA
# ℹ 3 more variables: RACIALIZED_7 <dbl>, RACIALIZED_8 <dbl>,
#   RACIALIZED_99 <dbl>


Nine columns cannot go into a table or a model as they are. The plan: count the boxes each person checked, then use case_when() to sort people into groups, putting anyone who checked two or more boxes into their own group instead of forcing them into one.

11.4.1 Step 1: count the checked boxes
!is.na() turns each cell into TRUE (checked) or FALSE (blank), and rowSums() adds up the TRUEs across the eight identity columns. RACIALIZED_99 is left out: declining to answer is not an identity.

mh_clean <- mh_clean |>
  mutate(RACIALIZED_N = rowSums(!is.na(across(RACIALIZED_1:RACIALIZED_8))))

mh_clean |> count(RACIALIZED_N)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  RACIALIZED_N     n
         <dbl> <int>
1            0     3
2            1   166
3            2    19




11.4.2 Step 2: sort people into groups: RACIALIZED_6CAT
The first condition that is true wins, so “two or more” has to come first; otherwise a person who checked Asian and White would land in whichever single-box line came first. Groups with very few people (codes 1, 5, 6, and 8) are combined into “Another identity”, because a group of three cannot support a comparison. factor() with levels = puts White first, which makes it the comparison group in every model later.

mh_clean <- mh_clean |>
  mutate(
    RACIALIZED_6CAT = factor(
      case_when(
        RACIALIZED_N >= 2     ~ "Two or more",
        !is.na(RACIALIZED_7)  ~ "White",
        !is.na(RACIALIZED_2)  ~ "Asian",
        !is.na(RACIALIZED_3)  ~ "Black",
        !is.na(RACIALIZED_4)  ~ "Hispanic or Latino",
        RACIALIZED_N == 1     ~ "Another identity"      # codes 1, 5, 6, 8: too few to stand alone
      ),
      levels = c("White", "Asian", "Black", "Hispanic or Latino", "Another identity", "Two or more")
    )
  )

# ALWAYS check a transformation
mh_clean |> count(RACIALIZED_6CAT)

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  RACIALIZED_6CAT        n
  <fct>              <int>
1 White                 94
2 Asian                 19
3 Black                 31
4 Hispanic or Latino    17
5 Another identity       5
6 Two or more           19
7 <NA>                   3

#source: The Quantitative Playbook for R (McCarty, 2026); R4DS Ch. 3 https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html
#explanation: people who checked two or more boxes become one group; single-box people are sorted by which box; the four smallest groups are combined; people who only declined get NA

People who checked only “Prefer not to say” match none of the conditions, so they get NA, which is what you want: a decline is missing, not a group.


11.4.3 Step 3: the binary version: RACIALIZED_01CAT
Many research questions compare people racialized as white with everyone else. Build the 0/1 version from RACIALIZED_6CAT, so the two variables can never disagree.

mh_clean <- mh_clean |>
  mutate(RACIALIZED_01CAT = case_when(RACIALIZED_6CAT == "White" ~ 0,
                                      !is.na(RACIALIZED_6CAT)    ~ 1))

mh_clean |> count(RACIALIZED_6CAT, RACIALIZED_01CAT)

# A tibble: 7 × 3
  RACIALIZED_6CAT    RACIALIZED_01CAT     n
  <fct>                         <dbl> <int>
1 White                             0    94
2 Asian                             1    19
3 Black                             1    31
4 Hispanic or Latino                1    17
5 Another identity                  1     5
6 Two or more                       1    19
7 <NA>                             NA     3

#source: The Quantitative Playbook for R (McCarty, 2026)
#explanation: 0 = racialized as white, 1 = racialized as a person of color (every other group, including Two or more); NA stays NA







CautionCaution: the name is RACIALIZED, and the binary is a teaching example



The variable is called RACIALIZED, not RACE, because the survey recorded how people are classified within a system of racial sorting, not a trait they carry (Fields & Fields, 2012; Zuberi & Bonilla-Silva, 2008; D’Ignazio & Klein, 2020; see Data Equity). When you report a result, write “people racialized as Black scored …”, not “Black people are …”. And RACIALIZED_01CAT is a coarse split that hides real differences between the groups it lumps together. It is here so that you can learn how a binary predictor works. A real report should also show RACIALIZED_6CAT.








GoGo: Name a new categorical variable for the number of groups it has



In this playbook, a variable made by cutting a score or collapsing categories ends in _#CAT, where # is the number of groups: DISTRESS_4CAT, EDUCATION_3CAT, HEALTH_3CAT, POL_3CAT, RACIALIZED_6CAT. A binary variable ends in _01CAT. It is either coded 0 and 1, or a factor with two levels, and either way the name says what the 1 (the second level) means: DISTRESS_01CAT (1 = likely distressed), RACIALIZED_01CAT (1 = racialized as a person of color, 0 = racialized as white). The name tells a reader what kind of variable it is before they look at a single value.








ImportantRequired: cite the cut-offs



If you cut a published scale into categories in your report, cite where the cut-offs come from, the way the K10 references below do. Cut-offs you chose yourself are okay if there is existing theory to inform the decision or for practical purposes, but you must report what you did transparently in your methods section and with your R code.

title: 6  Find the Ref
section: 6.4 Ref’s final whistle: before you quit RStudio
text:
6.4 Ref’s final whistle: before you quit RStudio
Keep counting. Steps 7 to 10 finish your session and back up your work.


Save your .qmd file (Cmd + S on Mac / Ctrl + S on Windows). If the file name at the top of the script editor is red with a *, it is not saved.
Render your .qmd file. To render means to turn your .qmd file into a finished report. Click the Render button, the blue arrow  at the top of the script editor. R then starts with an empty memory, runs all of your code from the first line to the last, and builds a report (a web page) with your writing, your plots, and your results. It can take a minute, and the report opens when it is done.

If the report appears, your code works from top to bottom. You will be able to pick up next time without surprises.
If it stops with an error, that is useful, too: it shows you the first line that does not work. If you cannot fix it today, type a note to yourself at that spot, starting with # (for example, # FIX: error on this line, object not found), so you know where to start next time.

Back up your files to your ELN. Open your individual ELN (your Google Drive folder) in your browser and open your R Labs folder. Click + New > File upload, go to your Lastname_FRI project folder, and select the files you worked on today: your .qmd files and your .R files (such as install.R). You can also drag the files from your project folder into the browser window. If Google Drive asks what to do with a file that is already there, choose Replace existing file. Google Drive keeps the older versions for you.
Quit RStudio. If RStudio asks to save your workspace, choose Don’t Save, because the workspace is the countertop, not the recipe. It holds the leftovers from today: your datasets and variables, including any made by code you later changed or deleted. If you save it, R puts those leftovers back the next time you open RStudio, and your results may no longer match your code. Your .qmd file and your data file are already saved, and they are all you need to make everything again.








CautionCaution: Save your file before you close RStudio



RStudio does not save your .qmd or .R file for you. If the file name on its tab is red with a *, your latest changes exist only on the screen, and closing RStudio throws them away. Two different questions come up when you quit, and they need opposite answers.
Do this

Press Cmd + S (Mac) or Ctrl + S (Windows) every few minutes, and always before you Render. The file name on the tab turns black when it is saved.
Before you quit, click File > Save All.
If RStudio asks “Save changes to report.qmd?”, click Save. That question is about your file.
Copy your .qmd and .R files to your ELN at the end of every session (Find the Ref).

Do not do this

Do not close RStudio, or your laptop, while a file name is still red.
Do not click Don’t Save when the question names a file (report.qmd, install.R). Only the question about the workspace (.RData) gets Don’t Save: the workspace is leftovers, and your file is the recipe.
Do not rely on Render to save for you. It usually does, but only for the file you rendered, and only if the render starts.










ImportantImportant: Close the project, reopen it, and run everything before you submit



Code that worked while you were editing can still fail from a clean start, because something you ran earlier by hand (a package, an object, a data file in the wrong place) was propping it up. Before you submit your RD Report or Final Report, and before you publish it, prove that it runs on its own:

Close the project: File > Close Project. If RStudio asks about the workspace, choose Don’t Save.
Open the project fresh: double-click Lastname_FRI.Rproj. The environment tab should be empty.
Run all of the code from the top. For a .qmd report, click Render; it starts a fresh R session and runs every chunk from the first line to the last, the same job Source does for an .R script.
Check the result. The report should open with every plot, table, and number in place, and the console should show no errors. If it stops, fix the first error, then start again from step 1.

Only when a fresh run works from top to bottom is the report ready to submit and publish. If it works on your computer this way, it will work on your peer mentor’s or Dr. Shane’s.








ImportantImportant: Your ELN is your backup



Laptops get lost, broken, and replaced. Your individual ELN is a Google Drive folder that does not. Get in the habit of backing up to your R Labs folder at the end of every work session, not only when something is due. A backup takes less than a minute. Redoing a lab or a report takes hours.

title: 6  Find the Ref
text:
6.8 You’re the quarterback
Ref calls the fouls, but Ref does not run the plays. You do. In this playbook you are the quarterback: the person in charge of carrying out the plan. Your peer mentors and Dr. Shane are your coaches. We wrote the playbook, we run the practices (the R Labs), and we are there to help. But a coach cannot play the game for you. When it is time to import your team’s data, build a composite, or run a model for your RD Report, you are the one who decides what to do and does it. The playbook shows you how; only you can do the work.
That takes a certain mindset. Coding is a way of thinking, not a list of commands to memorize. You will make mistakes, and that is normal: an error message tells you what to fix. It is not a judgment of whether you can do this. Every mistake in this playbook is correctable, and most take one line. You will also try things that do not work: a plot that does not show what you meant, a recode that puts people in the wrong group, a chunk that runs but answers a different question. None of that is wasted. Each one teaches you what the code actually does, which is exactly what you need to know.
You are not doing this alone. Come to R Lab with your questions, the error message on your screen, and the thing you tried. Check in with your peer mentor coaches when something is not working and problem-solve together; that is what lab time is for. Do not sit stuck for an hour on your own when three minutes with a coach would get you moving again. Ask early, ask often, and then go do it yourself.

title: 10  Pre/Post Data
text:
10.5 🏈 The Lab





Ref’s kickoff. This lab practices situation 1: one file in long format. The lab file ANTH306_LayConceptionsMH_SYNTHETIC_LONG.xlsx is the lab survey given twice, six weeks apart, and exported once. Every response is a row, TIME says 0 (pretest) or 1 (posttest), and PASSWORD links a person’s two rows. Try each step before you open my check.


Before you start. Get ANTH306_LayConceptionsMH_SYNTHETIC_LONG.xlsx from your instructor and put it in the data folder of your project. Open your lab .qmd, and run your load-library chunk (you need readxl, dplyr, and tidyr).

10.5.1 Lab Play 1: Import and look at the shape
Import the file as lab_long, then count the rows at each TIME. Look at the first rows: how many times does a person appear?






Go Ref’s check: how many rows?





324 rows in total: 200 pre (TIME = 0) and 124 post (TIME = 1). Not everyone came back, so there are fewer post rows than pre rows. That is normal.





10.5.2 Lab Play 2: Clean the password and look for duplicates
Make PASSWORD lowercase with no stray spaces, make TIME a factor with labels PRE and POST (PRE first), then count PASSWORD by TIME and filter to n > 1.






Go Ref’s check: any duplicates?





One: gl28fo appears twice at PRE. The same person submitted the pretest twice. Keep the first with distinct(PASSWORD, TIME, .keep_all = TRUE).





10.5.3 Lab Play 3: Reshape to wide
Keep PASSWORD, TIME, and HELPSEEK, then pivot_wider() so that each person has HELPSEEK_PRE and HELPSEEK_POST. Then count three things: people with both scores, people with only a pretest, and people with only a posttest.






Go Ref’s check: what should you get?






202 rows, one per PASSWORD.
114 people have both a pre and a post score. 81 have only a pretest (they did not come back). 10 have only a posttest.
Ten people with only a posttest is suspicious: everyone who took the posttest was supposed to have taken the pretest. Look at their passwords. Most are one character away from a pretest password (a typo). Real teams have to decide, and write down, whether to match those by hand. For the lab, leave them unmatched.










Resources👀 See the solution






library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

lab_long <- read_excel("data/ANTH306_LayConceptionsMH_SYNTHETIC_LONG.xlsx")
count(lab_long, TIME)                                 # Lab Play 1
head(lab_long)

lab_long <- lab_long |>                               # Lab Play 2
  mutate(PASSWORD = tolower(trimws(PASSWORD)),
         TIME = factor(TIME, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("PRE", "POST")))
lab_long |> count(PASSWORD, TIME) |> filter(n > 1)
lab_long <- lab_long |> distinct(PASSWORD, TIME, .keep_all = TRUE)

lab_wide <- lab_long |>                               # Lab Play 3
  select(PASSWORD, TIME, HELPSEEK) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = TIME, values_from = HELPSEEK, names_glue = "HELPSEEK_{TIME}")
nrow(lab_wide)
sum(!is.na(lab_wide$HELPSEEK_PRE) & !is.na(lab_wide$HELPSEEK_POST))   # both
sum(is.na(lab_wide$HELPSEEK_POST))                                     # pre only
sum(is.na(lab_wide$HELPSEEK_PRE))                                      # post only









Ref’s final whistle. Keep lab_wide and lab_long: Compare 1 Group, Pre/Post plots the long one, and the paired test (Compare 1 Group, Pre/Post, coming soon) uses the wide one. Save, render, back up to your ELN.

title: 13  Creating Composite Scores from Multi-Item Measures
text:
13.3 🏈 The Lab





Ref’s kickoff. The play used one dataset with two separate scales. Your team’s survey will have both kinds of multi-item measure: a unidimensional scale (one construct, one score, such as WELLBEING1 to WELLBEING8) and a multidimensional scale (one construct with subscales, such as stigma with public and self stigma). The lab practices both on the lab dataset, and ends with the sentence you will write in your Methods section. Try each play before you open my check.


Before you start. Open your lab .qmd, run your load-library chunk (psych must be loaded), and run source("lab_prep.R") so that mh_clean is in your environment. mh_clean already contains WELLBEING and STIGMA made with rowMeans(). In this lab you will make them again with scoreItems(), which also gives you the reliability.

13.3.1 Lab Play 1: A unidimensional scale (WELLBEING)
Positive mental well-being is measured with eight items, WELLBEING1 to WELLBEING8, all worded in the same direction, on a 1-to-5 frequency scale (none of the time to all of the time). Make a scoring key with one entry, run scoreItems() with impute = "none", read the alpha, and add the score to mh_clean as WELLBEING_SI. Then check that it equals the WELLBEING that lab_prep.R made.






ResourcesMissing answers: impute



When a participant skipped an item, scoreItems() fills in the item’s median for that person by default (impute = "median"). With impute = "none", it averages the items the person did answer, which is what rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) does. Both are defensible. Pick one for your report, use it for every composite, and say which one you used in your Methods.








Go Ref’s check: what should you find?






Cronbach’s alpha for WELLBEING is .81: good, by the table above.
No item is reverse-scored, so the key has no - signs.
all.equal() returns TRUE: with impute = "none", scoreItems() and rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) give the same average. The difference is that scoreItems() also reports reliability. (Leave out impute = "none" and the scores differ slightly for the people who skipped an item.)










Resources👀 See the solution






wb_keys <- list(WELLBEING = c("WELLBEING1", "WELLBEING2", "WELLBEING3", "WELLBEING4",
                              "WELLBEING5", "WELLBEING6", "WELLBEING7", "WELLBEING8"))
lab_wb <- scoreItems(wb_keys, mh_clean, impute = "none")
lab_wb                                     # alpha is in the first table

mh_clean$WELLBEING_SI <- lab_wb$scores[, "WELLBEING"]
all.equal(as.numeric(mh_clean$WELLBEING_SI), mh_clean$WELLBEING)   # same score as rowMeans()

#source: The Quantitative Playbook for R (McCarty, 2026); psych package (Revelle)
#explanation: one key with eight items, no reverse items; scoreItems() returns the mean of the eight items and Cronbach's alpha






13.3.2 Lab Play 2: A multidimensional scale (STIGMA with two subscales)
Stigma has eight items in two subscales: public stigma (STIGMA_PUB1 to STIGMA_PUB4_R) and self stigma (STIGMA_SELF1_R to STIGMA_SELF4_R). Three items end in _R: they are reverse items, stored in the original direction (Name and Recode Variables in Qualtrics), so they need a - in the key. Make a key with three entries, STIGMA_PUB, STIGMA_SELF, and STIGMA (all eight), run scoreItems(), and add all three scores to mh_clean. Then look at how the two subscales relate.






Go Ref’s check: what should you find?






Alphas: STIGMA_PUB = .72, STIGMA_SELF = .68, and the full STIGMA = .80. The eight-item total is more reliable than either four-item subscale. That is usual: alpha rises with the number of items, which is one reason to report the total as well as the subscales.
The two subscale scores correlate at r = .60: related, as parts of one construct should be, but far from identical, which is why the subscales are worth keeping.
If an alpha is much lower than these, or the output warns that some items correlate negatively with the total, you forgot a - on a reverse item. Fix the key and run it again.










Resources👀 See the solution






stig_keys <- list(
  STIGMA_PUB  = c("STIGMA_PUB1", "STIGMA_PUB2", "STIGMA_PUB3", "-STIGMA_PUB4_R"),
  STIGMA_SELF = c("-STIGMA_SELF1_R", "STIGMA_SELF2", "STIGMA_SELF3", "-STIGMA_SELF4_R"),
  STIGMA      = c("STIGMA_PUB1", "STIGMA_PUB2", "STIGMA_PUB3", "-STIGMA_PUB4_R",
                  "-STIGMA_SELF1_R", "STIGMA_SELF2", "STIGMA_SELF3", "-STIGMA_SELF4_R"))
lab_stig <- scoreItems(stig_keys, mh_clean, impute = "none")
lab_stig                                   # three alphas

mh_clean$STIGMA_PUB  <- lab_stig$scores[, "STIGMA_PUB"]
mh_clean$STIGMA_SELF <- lab_stig$scores[, "STIGMA_SELF"]
mh_clean$STIGMA      <- lab_stig$scores[, "STIGMA"]

cor(mh_clean$STIGMA_PUB, mh_clean$STIGMA_SELF, use = "complete.obs")

#source: The Quantitative Playbook for R (McCarty, 2026); psych package (Revelle)
#explanation: one key per subscale plus one for the total; the minus sign reverses the _R items before averaging; the subscale correlation shows they measure related but different parts of stigma






13.3.3 Lab Play 3: A scale that is summed, not averaged (the K10)
The ten DISTRESS items are the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10; Kessler et al., 2002), and Kessler’s scoring adds the items (10 to 50) instead of averaging them, because the published cut-offs are for the total (Transforming Your Data). scoreItems() can do that too: add totals = TRUE. (Keep the default impute here: a sum of only the answered items would be too low, and scoreItems() warns you about that.) Score the K10 and compare with K10_TOTAL from lab_prep.R.






Go Ref’s check: what should you find?






Alpha for the K10 is .87, good. Alpha is the same whether you sum or average: it depends on the items, not on the scoring.
With totals = TRUE, the scores run from 10 to 50 and equal K10_TOTAL for everyone who answered all ten items. The 23 people who skipped an item have NA in K10_TOTAL (rowSums() needs every item) but get a score from scoreItems(), which filled in the median. Say which rule you used.










Resources👀 See the solution






k10_keys <- list(K10 = paste0("DISTRESS", 1:10))     # the same as typing the ten names
lab_k10  <- scoreItems(k10_keys, mh_clean, totals = TRUE)
lab_k10
head(cbind(lab_k10$scores, mh_clean$K10_TOTAL))

#source: The Quantitative Playbook for R (McCarty, 2026); Kessler et al. (2002)
#explanation: totals = TRUE makes scoreItems() sum the items instead of averaging them, which is how the K10 is scored






13.3.4 Lab Play 4: Write the sentence for your Methods section
Every composite in your report needs one sentence in the Measures part of your Methods: what the scale measures, how many items, the response scale, how it was scored, any reverse items, and the reliability in this sample. Write those sentences for WELLBEING and STIGMA.






Go Ref’s check: a model sentence for each






Positive mental well-being was measured with eight items about the past two weeks (1 = none of the time to 5 = all of the time), averaged so that higher scores mean greater well-being (Cronbach’s α = .81).


Mental health stigma was measured with eight items on a 5-point agreement scale, in two subscales: public stigma (4 items, one reverse-scored; α = .72) and self stigma (4 items, two reverse-scored; α = .68). Reverse items were recoded before averaging, and the eight items were also averaged into a total stigma score (α = .80), with higher scores meaning more stigma. Scores were the mean of the items a participant answered.

Notice that a reader can rebuild your score from the sentence: number of items, direction, reverse items, averaging or summing, and the alpha you found, not the alpha in the original paper.








Ref’s final whistle. Put the sentences from Lab Play 4 in your coding journal: you will reuse their shape for your own measures. Save, render, back up to your ELN.

title: 13  Creating Composite Scores from Multi-Item Measures
text:
13.4 🏆 Your Turn






ResourcesThere is no Ref. It’s game time, your turn!



Score every multi-item measure in your team’s survey with scoreItems(), using your team codebook (Name and Recode Variables in Qualtrics) to tell you which items belong together, which are subscales, and which are reverse items. Then use the checklist.








GoGo: how long should a variable name be?



Aim for 6 to 10 characters for the measure’s name, and 14 or fewer for the whole tag including the subscale and the item number (AVOID_SLEEP1 is 12). That is short enough to read in a column header, in a plot legend, and in a line of R code, and long enough to be decoded without the codebook.
The tools will let you go longer, so the limit is readability, not software: R accepts names up to 10,000 characters, and Qualtrics only truncates an export tag when you export to SPSS, which cuts at 64. A name that needs 30 characters usually needs an abbreviation instead: Health Information Avoidance becomes AVOID, Kessler Psychological Distress becomes DISTRESS. Put the full name in your team codebook, where the variable name abbreviation gets explained once.



library(psych)

my_keys <- list(
  MEASURE    = c("ITEM1", "ITEM2", "-ITEM3_R", "ITEM4"),        # REPLACE: one entry per composite; - for reverse items
  SUBSCALE_A = c("ITEM1", "ITEM2"),                              # REPLACE: subscales, if your measure has them
  SUBSCALE_B = c("-ITEM3_R", "ITEM4")
)
my_scores <- scoreItems(my_keys, alldata, impute = "none")   # alldata = your team's imported .clean dataset
my_scores                                         # alpha for every entry in the key

alldata$MEASURE <- my_scores$scores[, "MEASURE"]  # REPLACE: add each score you will use








Criteria
Ask yourself




Items from the codebook
Does every entry in the key match the items listed for that measure in your team codebook, spelled exactly?


Reverse items
Does every item whose name ends in _R have a - in front of it, and no other item does?


Subscales and total
If the measure has subscales, did you score each subscale and the total?


Sum or mean
Did you score the way the published scale is scored (totals = TRUE for a summed scale such as the K10)?


Alpha
Is every alpha at least .70? If not, did you check the reverse items first, and then decide (and record) what to do?


Methods sentence
Does each composite have a Methods sentence with the number of items, response scale, direction, reverse items, scoring, and the alpha from your sample?


Score in the data
Did you add each score to alldata with a name that follows the naming rules (WELLBEING, STIGMA_PUB, not score1)?

title: 11  Transforming Your Data
section: 11.2 Example 1: Recoding Education Categories into Only 3 Education Categories
text:
11.2 Example 1: Recoding Education Categories into Only 3 Education Categories
When working with survey data, we often need to collapse detailed response categories into broader groups. This is useful for:

Simplifying analysis
Creating groups with adequate sample sizes
Making results easier to interpret


11.2.1 Original Education Variable
Our survey asked about education level with 7 response options:

Less than high school
High school diploma or GED
Some college, but no degree
Associate’s or technical degree
Bachelor’s degree
Master’s degree
Doctoral or professional degree



11.2.2 Recoding into Three Categories
Let’s group these into three meaningful categories:

# Create a new 3-category education variable
alldata <- alldata %>%
  mutate(
    EDUCATION_3CAT = factor(
      case_when(
        Education_Level %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4) ~ "Less than Bachelor's",
        Education_Level == 5 ~ "Bachelor's Degree",
        Education_Level %in% c(6, 7) ~ "Graduate Degree"
      ),
      levels = c("Less than Bachelor's", "Bachelor's Degree", "Graduate Degree")
    )
  )

# Check the recoding with a cross-tabulation
table(alldata$Education_Level, alldata$EDUCATION_3CAT, useNA = "ifany")

   
    Less than Bachelor's Bachelor's Degree Graduate Degree
  1                   11                 0               0
  2                   17                 0               0
  3                    8                 0               0

title: 11  Vignette Data
text:
11.1 Who needs this chapter?
This chapter is for Team 4 only. Team 4’s survey shows every participant four vignettes (short descriptions of a person) that are identical except for two details the team changed on purpose, and asks the same question after each one. The research question is a comparison between the four vignettes: does the rating change when the details change? Every other team has one rating per person and can skip this chapter.

title: 11  Vignette Data
text:
Resources📁 Team 4: four sentencing vignettes





Every participant reads four vignettes about a person convicted of the same crime and recommends a sentence after each: SENTENCE1 (racialized as Black, rich), SENTENCE2 (racialized as Black, poor), SENTENCE3 (racialized as White, rich), SENTENCE4 (racialized as White, poor). The lab dataset has the same design about mental health, so the Lab is your rehearsal, and Your Turn is your template.

title: 11  Vignette Data
section: 11.2 The idea: two factors, four vignettes, one row per rating
text:
11.2 The idea: two factors, four vignettes, one row per rating
When the same person rates several vignettes, each vignette is not a different person; it is a different condition. Two words describe that design:

A factor is a detail your team varied on purpose. Team 4 has two: racialized identity and class.
A level is one setting of a factor. Each of Team 4’s factors has two levels (Black / White; rich / poor).

Two factors with two levels each make 2 × 2 = 4 vignettes, one for every combination. Because every participant rates all four, the design is within-person (also called repeated measures): differences between the vignettes are measured inside each person, which is what makes the comparison fair, because the same people rate every vignette.
Qualtrics can only export this wide: one row per person and one column per vignette (CASE1 … CASE4 in the lab data). The column name tells you only the number. The analysis needs the data long: one row per person per vignette, with one column that says what the rating was and one column for each factor. This chapter gets you from the first shape to the second.

title: 11  Vignette Data
text:
11.3 The lab vignettes
The lab dataset asked every respondent the same question after four short vignettes (named CASE1 to CASE4 in the file): How likely is it that this person will be diagnosed with a serious mental illness in the next five years? (1 = very unlikely … 12 = very likely). The four vignettes are word-for-word the same except for two sentences.






Resources📄 Read the four vignettes





The shared part of every vignette. Jordan is 24 years old, works full time at a grocery store, and lives with two roommates. Jordan grew up in a small city, finished high school, and keeps in touch with family by phone most weeks.









Sentence that changes: racialized identity
Sentence that changes: current mental ill health




Case 1 (CASE1): Black, high
Jordan is Black.
Over the past six months, Jordan has had trouble sleeping most nights, has stopped seeing friends, has missed several shifts at work, and says that on some days it is hard to get out of bed.


Case 2 (CASE2): Black, low
Jordan is Black.
Over the past six months, Jordan has occasionally felt stressed about money and had a few restless nights, but sleeps well most of the time, sees friends on weekends, and has not missed work.


Case 3 (CASE3): White, high
Jordan is white.
(same as Case 1)


Case 4 (CASE4): White, low
Jordan is white.
(same as Case 2)



The question after each vignette. How likely is it that Jordan will be diagnosed with a serious mental illness in the next five years? 1 = very unlikely … 12 = very likely.
And then an open-ended one. Why did you rate Jordan’s risk this way? Its answers are in CASE1_QUAL to CASE4_QUAL, right after each rating, the way Team 4’s SENTENCE1_QUAL to SENTENCE4_QUAL follow each sentence. They are not used in this chapter; the mixed-methods chapter after Lab 6 brings the rating and the reason back together.



Notice how the four lab vignettes line up with Team 4’s: CASE1 is to SENTENCE1 as Black/high is to Black/rich, and so on down the list. That is on purpose, so that the code you write in the Lab is the code you will run in Your Turn.

title: 11  Vignette Data
text:
11.4 📋 The Play
The Play uses four made-up people so you can see every row.

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)


case_wide <- tibble(
  ResponseId = c("R_1a", "R_2b", "R_3c", "R_4d"),
  CASE1 = c(8, 5, 9, 6),     # racialized as Black, high
  CASE2 = c(9, 6, 10, 7),    # racialized as Black, low
  CASE3 = c(6, 4, 8, 5),     # racialized as White, high
  CASE4 = c(7, 5, 8, 6))     # racialized as White, low
case_wide

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  ResponseId CASE1 CASE2 CASE3 CASE4
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 R_1a           8     9     6     7
2 R_2b           5     6     4     5
3 R_3c           9    10     8     8
4 R_4d           6     7     5     6



11.4.1 Step 1: Write the design as a table
Before any code, write down which vignette is which combination. Take it from your survey and put it in your team codebook (Name and Recode Variables in Qualtrics). Everything below depends on it.



Column
CASE_RACIALIZED
CASE_SEVERITY




CASE1
Black
High


CASE2
Black
Low


CASE3
White
High


CASE4
White
Low



The factor names start with CASE_ so that a reader can tell them apart from the respondent’s own racialized identity (RACIALIZED_6CAT) and own distress (DISTRESS_4CAT), which are different variables about different people.


11.4.2 Step 2: pivot_longer(): one row per person per vignette
The four columns become two: CASE (which vignette the rating came from) and RISK (the rating). Each person now has four rows.

case_long <- case_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(CASE1, CASE2, CASE3, CASE4),
    names_to  = "CASE",
    values_to = "RISK")

case_long

# A tibble: 16 × 3
   ResponseId CASE   RISK
   <chr>      <chr> <dbl>
 1 R_1a       CASE1     8
 2 R_1a       CASE2     9
 3 R_1a       CASE3     6
 4 R_1a       CASE4     7
 5 R_2b       CASE1     5
 6 R_2b       CASE2     6
 7 R_2b       CASE3     4
 8 R_2b       CASE4     5
 9 R_3c       CASE1     9
10 R_3c       CASE2    10
11 R_3c       CASE3     8
12 R_3c       CASE4     8
13 R_4d       CASE1     6
14 R_4d       CASE2     7
15 R_4d       CASE3     5
16 R_4d       CASE4     6




11.4.3 Step 3: Add a factor for each thing that varied
CASE holds four labels, but the design has two factors. Use the table from Step 1 and case_when() (Transforming Your Data) to add them, and make each one a factor with the comparison level first: the level you will read the other one against.

case_long <- case_long |>
  mutate(
    CASE_RACIALIZED = factor(case_when(
      CASE %in% c("CASE1", "CASE2") ~ "Black",
      CASE %in% c("CASE3", "CASE4") ~ "White"),
      levels = c("White", "Black")),
    CASE_SEVERITY = factor(case_when(
      CASE %in% c("CASE1", "CASE3") ~ "High",
      CASE %in% c("CASE2", "CASE4") ~ "Low"),
      levels = c("Low", "High")))

case_long |> count(CASE, CASE_RACIALIZED, CASE_SEVERITY)   # ALWAYS check: 4 rows, each combination once

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  CASE  CASE_RACIALIZED CASE_SEVERITY     n
  <chr> <fct>           <fct>         <int>
1 CASE1 Black           High              4
2 CASE2 Black           Low               4
3 CASE3 White           High              4
4 CASE4 White           Low               4




11.4.4 Step 4: Check the reshape
Four vignettes times the number of people is the number of rows, and the count in Step 3 shows every vignette in exactly one combination of the two factors. If a combination appears twice or is missing, Step 1’s table and Step 3’s code disagree.

nrow(case_wide) * 4 == nrow(case_long)

[1] TRUE

case_long |>
  group_by(CASE_RACIALIZED, CASE_SEVERITY) |>
  summarise(mean_risk = mean(RISK), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  CASE_RACIALIZED CASE_SEVERITY mean_risk
  <fct>           <fct>             <dbl>
1 White           Low                6.5 
2 White           High               5.75
3 Black           Low                8   
4 Black           High               7   


The last table is the one your research question is about: the mean rating in each of the four cells. Whether those differences are more than chance is a test with two factors and repeated measures (every person rated all four vignettes), which is why ResponseId stays in the long data. That test comes in a later chapter; the data are now in the shape it needs.






GoGo: the same play, other designs



The same four steps work for three vignettes, for a 2 × 3 design, or for a repeated question that is not a vignette at all (the same rating of four messages, four policies, four treatments). What changes is the table in Step 1 and the case_when() lines that come from it.

title: 11  Vignette Data
text:
11.5 🏈 The Lab





Ref’s kickoff. The lab dataset has the four mental-health vignettes above as CASE1 to CASE4, one row per person. Run the four steps of the Play on mh_clean. Try each play before you open my check.


Before you start. Open your lab .qmd, run your load-library chunk (dplyr and tidyr), and run source("lab_prep.R") so that mh_clean is in your environment.

11.5.1 Lab Play 1: Look at the wide data
Select ResponseId and the four rating columns CASE1, CASE2, CASE3, CASE4 from mh_clean (name them one by one: the range CASE1:CASE4 would also pick up the _QUAL columns that sit between them) and look at the first rows and at summary() of the four columns.






Go Ref’s check: what should you see?






One row per person, 188 rows, and every rating between 1 and 12.
The means already tell the story: CASE1 (Black, high) is highest and CASE4 (White, low) is lowest. A few cells are NA: some people skipped a vignette.






11.5.2 Lab Play 2: Reshape to long and add the two factors
Do Steps 2 and 3 of the Play on the lab data, naming the result case_long, then count CASE by the two factors.






Go Ref’s check: what should you get?






752 rows: 188 people × 4 vignettes. nrow(mh_clean) * 4 == nrow(case_long) is TRUE.
The count has four rows, each vignette in exactly one cell, and each cell with 188 rows (the NA ratings are still rows; they just have no RISK).
levels(case_long$CASE_RACIALIZED) is White, Black, and levels(case_long$CASE_SEVERITY) is Low, High: the comparison level first.






11.5.3 Lab Play 3: The four cell means
Group case_long by the two factors and get the mean of RISK (with na.rm = TRUE) and the number of ratings in each cell.






Go Ref’s check: what should you find?









Low current ill health
High current ill health




Racialized as White
3.92
7.22


Racialized as Black
4.50
8.49




Current ill health moves the rating a lot (about 3.6 points): people rate the same future risk as much higher when the person is already struggling.
Holding ill health constant, the person described as Black is rated at higher risk than the person described as white, in both rows. The vignettes are otherwise word-for-word identical, so that difference is not about Jordan. It is about the raters, which is what makes a design like this useful for studying bias.
26 ratings are NA. na.rm = TRUE leaves them out of the means; a later test will decide how to handle people with a missing vignette.










Resources👀 See the solution






library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
source("lab_prep.R")

mh_clean |> select(ResponseId, CASE1, CASE2, CASE3, CASE4) |> head()          # Lab Play 1
summary(select(mh_clean, CASE1, CASE2, CASE3, CASE4))

case_long <- mh_clean |>                                        # Lab Play 2
  select(ResponseId, CASE1, CASE2, CASE3, CASE4) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(CASE1, CASE2, CASE3, CASE4), names_to = "CASE", values_to = "RISK") |>
  mutate(
    CASE_RACIALIZED = factor(case_when(
      CASE %in% c("CASE1", "CASE2") ~ "Black",
      CASE %in% c("CASE3", "CASE4") ~ "White"),
      levels = c("White", "Black")),
    CASE_SEVERITY = factor(case_when(
      CASE %in% c("CASE1", "CASE3") ~ "High",
      CASE %in% c("CASE2", "CASE4") ~ "Low"),
      levels = c("Low", "High")))
case_long |> count(CASE, CASE_RACIALIZED, CASE_SEVERITY)
nrow(mh_clean) * 4 == nrow(case_long)

case_long |>                                                    # Lab Play 3
  group_by(CASE_RACIALIZED, CASE_SEVERITY) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(RISK)), mean_risk = mean(RISK, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

#source: The Quantitative Playbook for R (McCarty, 2026); R4DS Ch. 5 https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html
#explanation: four vignette columns become one row per person per vignette; case_when() adds the two factors from the design table; the count proves each vignette is in one cell; the cell means are the descriptive answer to a 2 x 2 question










Caution Ref’s call: fouls to check if your numbers do not match






The count has more than four rows, or a cell is missing → a case_when() line names the wrong vignette. Compare the code with your Step 1 table, line by line.
nrow() is not four times the number of people → you selected more columns than the four vignettes into pivot_longer(), or fewer.
The means are all NA → you forgot na.rm = TRUE.
Levels come out alphabetically (Black before White) → you forgot levels = in factor().
An error about combining character and double (or RISK comes out as text) → you selected the _QUAL text columns along with the ratings, usually by writing a range like CASE1:CASE4. Name the four rating columns one by one.
object 'CASE1' not found → your lab data file is older than this chapter. Get the current ANTH306_LayConceptionsMH_SYNTHETIC.xlsx from your instructor.









Ref’s final whistle. Keep case_long: the two-factor test in a later chapter starts from it. Add the pivot_longer() and mutate() lines to the bottom of your lab_prep.R as case_long <- …. Save, render, back up to your ELN.

title: 11  Vignette Data
text:
11.6 🏆 Your Turn






ResourcesThere is no Ref. It’s game time, your turn!



Team 4: write your Step 1 table (which SENTENCE column is which vignette) into your codebook first, then change every line marked # REPLACE and use the checklist.



library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# 1. import the .clean file
alldata <- read_excel("data/10.09.2026.data.team4.clean.xlsx")   # REPLACE with your file
alldata[alldata == -99] <- NA
alldata[alldata == -50] <- NA

# 2. one row per person per vignette
case_long <- alldata |>
  select(ResponseId, SENTENCE1, SENTENCE2, SENTENCE3, SENTENCE4) |>   # REPLACE: name the rating columns one by one (a range would also grab the _QUAL columns)
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(SENTENCE1, SENTENCE2, SENTENCE3, SENTENCE4),   # REPLACE
    names_to  = "CASE",
    values_to = "SENTENCE")                           # REPLACE with the name of what was rated

# 3. add a factor for each thing the vignettes varied (from the Step 1 table in your codebook)
case_long <- case_long |>
  mutate(
    CASE_RACIALIZED = factor(case_when(
      CASE %in% c("SENTENCE1", "SENTENCE2") ~ "Black",     # REPLACE: which vignettes had which level
      CASE %in% c("SENTENCE3", "SENTENCE4") ~ "White"),
      levels = c("White", "Black")),
    CASE_CLASS = factor(case_when(
      CASE %in% c("SENTENCE1", "SENTENCE3") ~ "Rich",
      CASE %in% c("SENTENCE2", "SENTENCE4") ~ "Poor"),
      levels = c("Rich", "Poor")))

# 4. check: every vignette in exactly one cell; rows = people x vignettes; the four cell means
case_long |> count(CASE, CASE_RACIALIZED, CASE_CLASS)
nrow(alldata) * 4 == nrow(case_long)
case_long |>
  group_by(CASE_RACIALIZED, CASE_CLASS) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(SENTENCE)), mean_sentence = mean(SENTENCE, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")








Criteria
Ask yourself




Design table
Is the vignette-to-factor table in your codebook, and does every case_when() line match it?


One cell each
Does the count show each vignette in exactly one combination of the factors?


Row count
Is the number of rows the number of people times the number of vignettes?


Comparison level first
Did you set levels = so that the group you compare against comes first?


Names
Do the factor names start with CASE_, so they cannot be confused with the respondent’s own characteristics?


Person kept
Is ResponseId in the long data, so the test can tell whose ratings belong together?


Reported in methods
Does your Methods say every participant rated all four vignettes, in what order, and how many ratings were missing?










Resources Ref’s final whistle: before you quit RStudio





Save → Render → Back up to ELN → Quit, Don’t Save workspace. Details: Ref’s Quick Checklist.
